newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Prospect of holiday weighs on Belgian OLOs.
newsitem.headline: Prospect of holiday weighs on Belgian OLOs.

text.p: The prospect of a holiday in Belgium on Friday when key U.S. jobs data are due has squeezed OLOs into a tight range pattern which is unlikely to be unlocked in the next two trading sessions, dealers said.
"We're going to see the same pattern for the rest of the week," one trader said.
At 1440 GMT, the benchmark 2006 OLO was yielding 6.13 percent, down from 6.16 percent in the morning and compared with 6.11 percent at the close on Monday.
OLOs recovered in line with Bunds, the 10-year yield spread unchanged from opening levels at 10 bp against nine Monday.

One trader expected Belgium to fall behind Germany in its recovery and the spread to widen somewhat if market belief started spreading that the convergence criteria laid down by the Maastricht Treaty would be made more flexible to suit Germany.

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said earlier that a forecast made by Germany's six leading economic institutes that Germany might fail to meet the current Maastricht debt and deficit criteria might be realistic.
Traders said the curve has been flattening since Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said last Wednesday there was no reason to expect further cuts in key German interest rates.
"But I don't buy that," one trader said.
He said the short end of the curve was under considerable selling pressure but was unlikely to break out of its range.
Monday's OLO auction at which a higher-than-expected 28 billion francs were sold had no major impact on the market, but there was no follow-up buying at today's non-competitive auction.
Another domestic factor which was largely ignored was a 24-hour strike by the socialist trade union on Monday.
Some traders said that the market would be underpinned by the continued absence of domestic institutional sellers.
They said Belgian institutionals were reluctant to sell because of the taxation of realized capital gains.
"They would be fiscally punished if they sold any further," one said.
He estimated that 95 percent of Belgian debt was in Belgian hands, compared with between 70 and 80 percent in France.
"If you see how much France is influenced by domestic players...it's even worse here and certainly worse than in Bunds or Treasuries which are being traded by everyone," he said.
